goal.text: Students prepare for and conduct a negotiation by separating interests from positions, identifying their BATNA, and proposing options that create value for both sides

learnerRole.text: Advise a colleague who is about to negotiate a job offer, and help them plan what to ask for and why

character.name: Dana Okafor
character.role: a nervous colleague, two years out of college, who has a job offer in hand and wants to be told what number to ask for

materials.name: Lecture notes week 3
materials.text: A position is what a party says they want; an interest is the reason they want it. Two parties can hold opposed positions while having compatible interests. Skilled negotiators ask why before they ask how much. Your BATNA is your best alternative to a negotiated agreement: what you will do if this negotiation fails. The BATNA determines your reservation price, the point at which you are better off walking away. A strong BATNA gives you leverage; a weak BATNA should be improved before you negotiate, not revealed during it. The zone of possible agreement, or ZOPA, lies between the two reservation prices. Value is created when parties trade issues they value differently: a candidate may value a later start date or remote days more than the employer values granting them. Splitting the difference on a single issue such as salary only divides value; adding issues such as start date, signing bonus, title, or review timing can create value for both sides. Revealing your bottom line early anchors the discussion at your worst acceptable outcome.

stakes.text: the colleague will either accept a weak offer immediately or blurt out their bottom line and damage the relationship with their future manager

criteria.text: Distinguishes the underlying interests of each party from their stated positions

activation: Before you begin: in your own words, what do you already know about "Salary negotiation: interests before positions"?
Which idea from earlier lessons do you expect to need most here, and why?

practice.opening: Hi, I'm Dana Okafor. Thanks for making time. I really need your help with this.

challenges.prompt: Where would you start with my situation?
challenges.harder: That helps. But this matters a lot to me, so let me push: why are you sure? What would make you change your advice?
support: Can you say a bit more about what you're basing that on?
Maybe look back at the course material from before we started. Is there a part of it that helps here?

practice.ack: That's useful, it covers something I was going to ask about.

probes.voice: I've always heard that the best opening move is to state your bottom line so nobody wastes time. Any reason I shouldn't go with that?
probes.challenge: Hold on. You said something that sounded like "the best opening move is to state your bottom line so nobody wastes time". If that were true, what would we expect to see? Does that match what you know?

probes.voice: I've always heard that negotiation is a fixed pie where every gain for one side is a loss for the other. Any reason I shouldn't go with that?
probes.challenge: Hold on. You said something that sounded like "negotiation is a fixed pie where every gain for one side is a loss for the other". If that were true, what would we expect to see? Does that match what you know?

practice.closing: All right. I have what I need to decide. Thank you for your time.
practice.closingUnsure: Thanks for your time. I'm still not sure what to do, so I'll think about it some more.
practice.refusal: I can't answer that for you. Your judgement is exactly what I came for. Start with what you're surest of.

selfAssessment: Before you see any feedback: how do you think that went? Which moment are you most satisfied with?
What would you do differently if you did it again?
feedback.transfer: A different situation: negotiating project deadlines and resources with another team inside your own company. What from this session would you use there, and what would you change?
